html.p: Both chart types convey statistical distribution rather than a single point value. The candlestick (OHLC) chart originates in financial analysis but applies equally to any metric where you track open, close, minimum, and maximum over a period. The boxplot is a classical statistical chart for comparing distributions across categories.

Each candlestick is defined by four values in the order [open, close, lowest, highest]. ECharts colours the body green (rising) or red (falling) automatically based on whether close > open or close < open.

In Splunk, if your search produces OHLC columns you can bind them with seriesDataIndexBinding=[col_open;col_close;col_low;col_high]. The example below uses static data to keep the focus on the option structure:
Set yAxis: { scale: true } so the y-axis starts at the data range rather than zero — essential for financial-style charts.

html.p: A common pattern is overlaying a moving average line on a candlestick chart. Add a line series alongside the candlestick series, sharing the same xAxis. Both series use the same x-axis category labels; the line series provides its own data with the pre-computed MA values:
Note: set the first N-1 MA values to null to avoid plotting before enough data points exist for the window.

html.p: A boxplot represents a statistical distribution using five summary statistics per category: minimum, first quartile (Q1), median, third quartile (Q3), and maximum. ECharts expects each data entry as [min, Q1, median, Q3, max].
This is well suited for comparing response-time distributions across services, error rates across hosts, or any metric where you want to show spread rather than just the mean.

To compute these statistics in Splunk, combine eventstats or streamstats with perc25(), median(), perc75(), min(), and max() aggregation functions, then bind via seriesDataIndexBinding=[min_col;q1_col;median_col;q3_col;max_col].
